title: Innovation Requires Subtraction
author: Molly Graham
summary: Molly Graham reports on a day spent at X, Alphabet's Moonshot Factory, and a conversation with its leader Astro Teller about building a culture that reliably produces innovation. She offers three takeaways. First, stop confusing progress with learning: teams must identify the riskiest part of a project, the monkey reciting Shakespeare, rather than building the easy pedestal. Second, get good at proving yourself wrong, as when Teller had the Wing team imagine a failed launch and list why it failed. Third, make it easier to stop things, since organizations add projects far more readily than they remove them. X reinforces this with failure resumes and ceremonies that mourn and celebrate killed projects. Graham argues that a leader's reaction to bad news defines culture more than any statement about innovation.
points: Tackle the riskiest part of a project first, because building the easy parts only looks like progress.
Reward people for finding out what is true, using exercises like imagining a failed launch and listing the reasons it failed.
Make stopping a project a respected outcome, since organizations add much more easily than they subtract.
Leaders define culture by how they react when someone reports a year of work has failed.
A culture of innovation must be as willing to let go of ideas as to generate them.
quotes: If you are not committed to de-stigmatizing failure, you are not really committed to learning fast because the tightest learning loops are the ones that have the most failures in them.
His point is that if you were given that project, most people start by building the pedestal. Because it’s easy, you know how to do it, and you can show your boss that you’re making progress.
It’s easy to spend enormous amounts of time doing work that looks like progress without answering the questions that actually determine whether something will succeed.
Astro’s point is that most of us have spent our careers being rewarded for getting the right answer. He is trying to build a culture where people are rewarded for finding out what’s actually true.
Inside companies, we add projects, priorities, teams, processes, and products. But once something exists, people become attached to it.
Telling people to be intellectually honest isn’t enough. You have to create an environment where they can admit something isn’t working without feeling like they’ve failed.
Your reaction in that moment will define your culture far more than anything you say about innovation.
A huge part of the discipline of innovation is building an organization that's as willing to let go of ideas as it is to come up with them.
